case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act authorizes a private federal cause of action for contracting parties to seek rescission of contracts alleged to violate the Act.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Investment Company Act of 1940, Section 47(b), 15 U.S.C. § 80a-46(b) (especially § 80a-46(b)(2)).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that ICA § 47(b) does not create a private right of action; it is a remedial/contract-validity provision that presupposes enforcement through other ICA mechanisms (primarily SEC enforcement and the Act’s express private remedies). Under the Court’s implied-rights framework (e.g., Sandoval), a private cause of action cannot be inferred absent clear rights-creating text and structural evidence of congressional intent, and recognizing such a remedy would improperly expand private litigation in a statute where Congress largely limited private enforcement.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that the plain text of § 47(b)(2) affirmatively contemplates suit by private parties to illegal contracts to obtain rescission (i.e., to void/undo the contract), making rescission available as a federal remedy when a contract violates the ICA. They emphasize that this is a narrow remedy (rescission/voiding, not compensatory damages) and that recognizing it aligns with the statutory language and the Court’s approach in analogous statutes that render illegal contracts void.
key_precedents: Northwest Airlines, Inc. v. Transport Workers Union of America, 451 U.S. 77 (1981)
Touche Ross & Co. v. Redington, 442 U.S. 560 (1979)
Transamerica Mortgage Advisors, Inc. v. Lewis (TAMA), 444 U.S. 11 (1979)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson make the best textual point that “a court may not deny rescission at the instance of any party” sounds like it anticipates an affirmative request, but under Sandoval and Touche Ross that sort of court-directed remedial language still does not supply the distinct, rights-creating congressional decision to authorize a freestanding private suit. The better reading—consistent with Justice Kagan’s structural argument—is that §47(b)(2) presupposes some proper vehicle bringing the illegality before a court (SEC action, an express ICA private action, or defensive/counterclaim posture) and then limits the court’s remedial discretion, rather than creating new federal jurisdiction by implication. Transamerica does not genuinely undermine that conclusion because it rested on materially different “void” language and predates our modern clear-statement approach to implied causes of action; at most it shows rescission can be an available remedy once a claim is otherwise properly in court. A narrow holding that §47(b)(2) does not itself create a private right of action, while leaving open its use as a defense/counterclaim and as a remedial rule in authorized proceedings, best respects precedent and institutional restraint.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the hardest textual point: “a court may not deny rescission at the instance of any party” sounds like it anticipates an affirmative request. But under Sandoval and Touche Ross, court-directed remedial language—even with party-invoking phrasing—does not answer the antecedent question whether Congress created a freestanding cause of action; it more naturally functions as a rule of decision once illegality is established through an authorized vehicle (including express ICA private actions, SEC enforcement, or defensive litigation). Justice Sotomayor’s surplusage concern is not enough to overcome the ICA’s structure, which elsewhere uses clear rights-creating language to authorize private suits and thus counsels against inferring an additional one from §47(b)’s remedial constraint. Transamerica, as Justice Roberts notes, rests on materially different “void” language and predates our modern clear-statement approach, so it does not undermine my textualist/originalist conclusion here.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson make their best point from the phrase “at the instance of any party,” but under Sandoval and Touche Ross that kind of court-directed remedial command still does not supply the distinct, rights-creating authorization to file a freestanding federal suit. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, §47(b)(2) reads more naturally as a limit on a court’s remedial discretion once illegality is properly before it—whether via SEC enforcement, an express ICA private provision, or defensively—rather than an implicit jurisdiction-conferring cause of action. Their reliance on Transamerica is not enough to overcome the ICA’s structure and our modern clear-statement approach, since Transamerica turned on materially different “void” language and predated Sandoval’s stricter methodology. Practical concerns about making the clause “inert” cannot justify implying a new private action where Congress chose selective express remedies in a scheme centered on administrative enforcement.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s Sandoval/Touche Ross point—that court-directed remedial language does not itself create a cause of action—has force, and I agree we should not expand § 47(b) into a broad private-enforcement regime. But the specific phrasing Congress chose in § 47(b)(2)—“a court may not deny rescission at the instance of any party”—is unusually party-invoking and reads most naturally to contemplate an affirmative invocation by a contracting party, not merely a remedial constraint in someone else’s suit; otherwise, as Justice Jackson notes, the clause risks becoming practically inert for investors lacking any realistic procedural vehicle to get into court. The colleagues’ attempt (Justice Kagan, Justice Barrett) to cabin the language to SEC actions or defensive postures does not answer why Congress would speak in mandatory terms about what a court may not do “at the instance of any party” if parties could never initiate that request. Transamerica’s recognition of a narrow rescission remedy for unlawful contracts supports reading § 47(b) to carry a similarly limited, contract-unwinding private action—narrow enough to respect Sandoval’s caution while still giving effect to Congress’s operative language.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson are right to focus on the phrase “at the instance of any party,” which sounds like it anticipates a party affirmatively asking for rescission. But under Sandoval and Touche Ross, even party-invoking, court-directed remedial language is not the same as rights-creating text that authorizes a new federal cause of action; it more naturally functions as a rule of decision that limits a court’s discretion once some proper vehicle (SEC action, an express ICA private claim, or even a defense/counterclaim) puts illegality before the court. Their reliance on Transamerica does not overcome the ICA’s structural cue—selective express private remedies elsewhere—that Congress knew how to create private suits and did so only in specified places, and Transamerica’s “void” language and pre-Sandoval methodology make it a poor fit here. Pragmatically, I share Justice Roberts’s concern that treating §47(b) as jurisdiction-creating would expand private litigation in a calibrated scheme without the clear textual commitment our modern cases demand.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the hardest textual point: “a court may not deny rescission at the instance of any party” sounds like it anticipates an affirmative request. But under Sandoval and Touche Ross, court-directed remedial language—even coupled with “any party”—does not itself supply the separate, rights-creating congressional decision to authorize a freestanding federal cause of action; it more naturally operates as a rule of decision limiting equitable discretion once illegality is properly before a court through an authorized vehicle (including SEC enforcement or a defense/counterclaim). As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas note, Transamerica is materially distinguishable because it rested on “void” language and pre-dates our clear-statement approach to implied rights; it cannot overcome the ICA’s structural cue that Congress expressly created private actions in some sections and otherwise relied on SEC-centered enforcement. The fairness concerns are real, but they cannot substitute for the textual authorization our precedents require before we expand private litigation in a calibrated regulatory scheme.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson make the best textual point: “may not deny rescission at the instance of any party” sounds like an affirmative invocation. But under Sandoval and Touche Ross, that kind of court-directed remedial constraint still does not answer the antecedent question whether Congress created a freestanding private cause of action; it is fully coherent, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan argue, to read §47(b)(2) as a rule of decision governing rescission once illegality is properly before a court through some authorized vehicle (including SEC enforcement or defensive/counterclaim posture). Transamerica does not genuinely undermine that conclusion because it rested on materially different “void” language and a different implied-rights methodology, whereas the ICA’s structure—selective express private remedies alongside SEC-centered enforcement—counsels against silently expanding private litigation. Institutionally and practically, implying a new cause of action here would be a significant step with real consequences for the regulatory scheme, and our precedents require clearer congressional authorization than this.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the hardest point: “a court may not deny rescission at the instance of any party” sounds like an affirmative invitation to sue. But under Sandoval and Touche Ross, party-invoking or remedial language aimed at courts does not itself supply the distinct, rights-creating congressional decision to authorize a new private cause of action; it more naturally functions as a rule of decision once illegality is properly before a court through an authorized vehicle. Justice Kagan’s structural point reinforces that reading: the ICA includes selective, express private remedies and otherwise relies on SEC-centered enforcement, making it unlikely Congress silently created an additional, freestanding federal rescission action in §47(b). Transamerica does not undermine that conclusion because it turned on materially different “void” language and pre-Sandoval implied-rights methodology, whereas §47(b)(2) can do work as a remedial constraint without creating jurisdiction or a new claim.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s Sandoval/Touche Ross point seriously that court-directed remedial language often presupposes an existing cause of action, and Justice Kagan’s structural warning about the ICA’s selective express remedies is the hardest counterweight. But §47(b)(2)’s command that a court “may not deny rescission at the instance of any party” is unusually party-invoking and, in ordinary legal usage, contemplates an affirmative request by a litigant—not merely a defense that happens to arise in some other suit—and reading it as purely remedial risks draining that phrase of practical meaning for injured investors who otherwise lack a procedural vehicle. Transamerica is not controlling, and I accept it predates our modern implied-rights methodology, yet it remains persuasive on the narrower proposition that when Congress speaks in contract-invalidity terms, the customary incident is a rescission remedy; recognizing only that limited rescission action (not damages) respects Sandoval’s concern about expansive private enforcement while giving §47(b)(2) operative effect. On pragmatic, procedure-centered grounds, I am not persuaded that Congress wrote mandatory, party-triggered language merely to guide judges in the relatively rare subset of cases already before them through other ICA mechanisms or SEC actions.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under this Court’s implied-rights framework, a private federal cause of action exists only where Congress clearly manifested that intent in rights-creating text and statutory structure. Section 47(b)(2)’s direction that a “court may not deny rescission at the instance of any party” is most naturally read as governing the availability and standards for rescission when illegality under the ICA is properly before a court (including defensively), not as creating a freestanding private enforcement mechanism—especially given the ICA’s selective, express private remedies elsewhere, which counsels against implying additional ones. Alexander v. Sandoval and Touche Ross instruct that remedial language cannot substitute for a clear congressional decision to authorize suit, and recognizing a new private cause here would expand litigation in a sensitive regulatory scheme without the requisite textual commitment. Transamerica Mortgage Advisors is distinguishable because it turned on a “void” declaration with customary incidents of voidness; § 47(b) is framed as a remedial rule for rescission rather than an express rights-conferring authorization to sue.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 47(b) is framed as a contract-validity and remedial directive (“a court may not deny rescission”), not as rights-creating language conferring an entitlement to sue; under Sandoval and Touche Ross, a private federal cause of action must be grounded in clear textual evidence of congressional intent. The Act’s overall structure—express enforcement authority in the SEC and limited express private remedies elsewhere—cuts against inferring an additional private cause of action from §80a-46(b)(2). Unlike provisions that expressly create liability, §47(b) presupposes some proper enforcement vehicle and then constrains the rescission remedy once a violation is established, which is insufficient to create a freestanding private right. To the extent Transamerica Mortgage Advisors recognized a limited rescission remedy under the IAA’s different text, that inference cannot be extended here absent comparably explicit rights-creating terms in the ICA.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 47(b) speaks in remedial/contract-validity terms and lacks the sort of rights-creating language that, under Alexander v. Sandoval and Touche Ross, is necessary to infer a private federal cause of action. The phrase in §47(b)(2) that “a court may not deny rescission at the instance of any party” is most naturally read as a limitation on courts’ remedial discretion once some properly authorized enforcement action is before them, not as an affirmative grant of a freestanding private right to sue. Congress provided express enforcement mechanisms elsewhere in the ICA, and recognizing an implied rescission action here would expand private litigation beyond what the statute’s structure indicates Congress intended. Transamerica (TAMA) does not compel a different result because it involved distinct statutory language in the IAA and, consistent with Sandoval’s approach, does not justify implying broader private enforcement absent clear textual authorization.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 47(b)(2) provides that “a court may not deny rescission at the instance of any party” absent specified equitable findings, language that most naturally presupposes an affirmative ability of contracting parties to seek rescission in federal court rather than merely raise it defensively. That reading is reinforced by Transamerica Mortgage Advisors, Inc. v. Lewis, 444 U.S. 11 (1979), which recognized an implied private right to equitable rescission under the Investment Advisers Act’s closely analogous “voiding” provision, and by Congress’s subsequent choice to make § 47(b) even more explicit about rescission’s availability and limits. While Sandoval cautions against implying broad private damages remedies absent clear rights-creating text, the narrow, equitable rescission remedy in § 47(b) fits the statute’s investor-protection purpose and ensures meaningful relief for parties harmed by unlawful investment-company contracts, especially where agency enforcement may be inadequate for vulnerable investors.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 47(b) supplies a remedial rule about the availability of rescission once a party is properly before a court, but it does not contain the kind of rights-creating language that, under Alexander v. Sandoval, is required to infer a new private federal cause of action. The phrase in § 47(b)(2) that a court may not deny rescission “at the instance of any party” can operate as a constraint on judicial discretion in cases brought under other ICA enforcement mechanisms (including the Act’s express private remedies) or as a defense/claim in existing litigation, without implying a freestanding federal suit. Transamerica Mortgage Advisors, Inc. v. Lewis supports treating “void/unenforceable contract” language as authorizing rescission in appropriate cases but cautions against inferring broader private enforcement absent clear textual direction—especially here, where the ICA contains specific express private causes of action, suggesting Congress knew how to authorize private suits when it wished. Given the ICA’s structure and Sandoval’s clear-statement approach, recognizing a new implied cause of action from § 47(b) would be an unwarranted expansion of private litigation.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 47(b) speaks in remedial terms about when a contract is unenforceable and when a court may not deny rescission “at the instance of any party,” 15 U.S.C. § 80a-46(b)(2), but it nowhere uses rights-creating language authorizing a plaintiff to sue, and under Sandoval we do not invent private causes of action absent clear textual evidence. The clause can do work without creating a cause of action—by supplying a uniform federal rule for rescission when parties are already properly before a court (e.g., as an affirmative defense or in an SEC-initiated enforcement context). The Act’s structure reinforces that reading because Congress provided express private remedies elsewhere in the ICA, counseling against implying additional ones. TAMA does not compel the opposite result because it rested on materially different statutory language in IAA § 215(b) and cannot overcome the ICA’s text-and-structure limits on private enforcement here.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under this Court’s implied-rights framework, the question is congressional intent as reflected in text and structure, and Section 47(b) lacks the kind of rights-creating language that Sandoval and Touche Ross require to recognize a new private federal cause of action. Section 47(b)(2)’s direction that “a court may not deny rescission at the instance of any party” can do substantial work without creating an affirmative cause of action—e.g., supplying uniform federal rescission rules when rescission is sought defensively or in cases properly before a court through some other enforcement mechanism. Unlike the Investment Advisers Act provision at issue in Transamerica Mortgage Advisors (which declared certain contracts “void” and was construed to carry customary incidents of voidness), the ICA’s overall structure includes express private remedies elsewhere, reinforcing that Congress did not silently authorize additional private suits via § 47(b). Practical workability and institutional restraint also counsel against expanding private litigation where Congress largely channeled enforcement through the SEC and specific express causes of action.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 47(b) speaks in remedial and contract-validity terms (“a court may not deny rescission at the instance of any party” when an illegal contract “has been performed,” 15 U.S.C. § 80a-46(b)(2)), but it does not contain the kind of rights-creating language or an express cause-of-action grant that this Court requires before recognizing private enforcement. Under Alexander v. Sandoval, the question is whether Congress displayed an intent to create a private cause of action, and the ICA’s structure—express private remedies in §§ 30(h) and 36(b) alongside broad SEC-centered enforcement for other violations—cuts against implying another. Read textually, § 47(b)(2) supplies a rule of decision about when rescission is available (and limits courts’ discretion once rescission is properly sought), but it can operate in SEC actions or as a defense without creating a freestanding private federal suit. Touche Ross reinforces that where Congress “knew how” to create private actions and did so expressly, courts should not infer additional ones from remedial language alone.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 47(b)(2) speaks in expressly judicial, party-invoking terms—“a court may not deny rescission at the instance of any party” absent specified equitable findings—language that most naturally presupposes that contracting parties may affirmatively seek rescission in federal court, not merely raise it defensively. In Transamerica Mortgage Advisors, Inc. v. Lewis, 444 U.S. 11 (1979), the Court recognized a limited private remedy for rescission where Congress rendered unlawful contracts void/unenforceable, and § 47(b) is the ICA’s parallel contract-invalidity and rescission provision. While Sandoval cautions against implying broad private enforcement absent clear congressional intent, recognizing a narrow rescission action tied to an illegal contract’s validity is consistent with the statute’s text and structure and promotes procedural fairness by ensuring parties are not left without a practical mechanism to unwind unlawful arrangements. Limiting the remedy to rescission (rather than damages) also mitigates concerns about expanding private litigation beyond what Congress contemplated.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act implicitly authorizes private plaintiffs to bring a federal cause of action for rescission of contracts alleged to violate the Act.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Investment Company Act of 1940, Section 47(b), 15 U.S.C. § 80a-46(b) (especially § 80a-46(b)(2)).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that Section 47(b) does not create (and cannot be read to imply) a private federal cause of action for rescission because the ICA’s text and structure do not contain the rights-creating language and affirmative congressional intent required under this Court’s modern implied-right-of-action doctrine. In their view, Section 47(b) is a remedial/contract-validity provision that may describe consequences of illegality or defenses, but it does not confer a privately enforceable right to sue; recognizing such a cause of action would improperly expand private ICA litigation beyond what Congress authorized, particularly given the ICA’s express enforcement mechanisms and limited express private remedies elsewhere in the statutory scheme.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that Section 47(b)(2)’s plain text contemplates that parties may 'seek rescission' (i.e., unwind/void) illegal contracts, and that the most natural reading is that Congress authorized a limited private remedy of rescission (not damages) for contracting parties. They contend this is consistent with the statute’s structure and with precedent recognizing limited contract-voiding remedies in analogous federal securities statutes, and that petitioners’ approach would read the rescission language as largely ineffectual. Respondents also emphasize that modern implied-right-of-action principles allow implication where text and structure demonstrate congressional intent, and that here the language is sufficiently rights- and remedy-directive to support a narrow rescission action.
key_precedents: Northwest Airlines, Inc. v. Transport Workers Union of America, 451 U.S. 77 (1981)
Touche Ross & Co. v. Redington, 442 U.S. 560 (1979)
Transamerica Mortgage Advisors, Inc. v. Lewis (TAMA), 444 U.S. 11 (1979)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor presses the strongest counterargument: that “may not deny rescission at the instance of any party” most naturally presupposes an affirmative ability to sue, and that reading it as inert risks draining the phrase of meaning. But as Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan explain, under Sandoval and Touche Ross remedial, court-directed language—even if it assumes parties will request relief—does not clearly create the separate, antecedent element Congress must supply: a freestanding cause of action; it can instead operate as a mandatory rule of decision once rescission is properly before a court through some other jurisdictional or claim vehicle. Transamerica, while relevant, does not genuinely upset that analysis because it relied on different “void” language and predates our more demanding clear-statement approach to implied causes of action, and the ICA’s structure (including its selective express private remedy in §36(b) and SEC-centered enforcement) counsels against implying an additional suit. A narrow holding—§47(b) does not itself create a private right of action, while leaving rescission available when a case is otherwise properly in court—best accommodates the opposing textual point without expanding private enforcement beyond what Congress clearly authorized.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is textual: §47(b)(2)’s “may not deny rescission at the instance of any party” sounds like party-invoked judicial relief, and she warns that reading it as merely “inert” risks draining the phrase of meaning. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett explain, under Sandoval and Touche Ross remedial, court-directed language—even if it presupposes a party request—does not itself supply the distinct, rights-creating text needed to authorize a freestanding federal cause of action; it can operate as a mandatory rule of decision once rescission is properly before a court via some other vehicle. Transamerica does not alter that conclusion because it relied on materially different “void” language and predates our modern insistence on clear congressional creation of private enforcement, especially in a statute like the ICA with an SEC-centered scheme and a selective express private remedy in §36(b). On an original public meaning and structural reading, I cannot treat §47(b)’s remedial constraint on courts as silent authorization for new federal suits.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that “may not deny rescission at the instance of any party” sounds like party-invoked litigation and risks becoming surplusage if no affirmative action exists. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, Sandoval and Touche Ross require clear rights-creating language to infer a freestanding federal cause of action, and §47(b)(2) reads more naturally as a court-directed remedial constraint that operates once rescission is properly before a court through some other claim or jurisdictional vehicle (including defensive invocation). Transamerica does not genuinely undermine that conclusion because, as Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch note, it rested on materially different “void” language and arose in a pre-Sandoval era; extending it here would be an unwarranted expansion in light of the ICA’s SEC-centered enforcement scheme and Congress’s selective express private remedy in §36(b). Under a textualist approach attentive to our modern implied-right precedents and practical consequences for enforcement design, I remain persuaded §47(b) supplies a rule of decision about rescission, not an implied authorization for new federal suits.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point seriously: Sandoval and Touche Ross demand clear congressional creation of a cause of action, and remedial language can sometimes operate as a rule of decision once a case is otherwise properly in court. But §47(b)(2) is unusually party-centered—“may not deny rescission at the instance of any party”—and that phrasing most naturally presupposes an affirmative ability of contracting parties to invoke rescission, not merely to benefit from it incidentally when some other claim supplies a vehicle. Justice Barrett’s proposed “rule-of-decision only” reading risks rendering that party-initiated language largely inert in precisely the circumstances where SEC enforcement gaps leave investors without meaningful relief, and Transamerica remains persuasive in the limited sense that Congress’s specification of rescission and constraint of judicial discretion is strong textual evidence of an available, cabined equitable action. Given the ICA’s structure, I would keep the remedy narrow (equitable rescission/unwinding, not damages), but I do not think our modern implied-right cases require us to treat §47(b)(2)’s party-invocation text as having no operative private enforcement content.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that “may not deny rescission at the instance of any party” sounds like Congress contemplated a party affirmatively seeking rescission, and that reading §47(b)(2) as merely a background rule risks making that phrase feel underpowered. But under Sandoval and Touche Ross, that kind of court-directed remedial command—however party-inviting—still doesn’t supply the missing, rights-creating ingredient: an authorization for a private plaintiff to sue in federal court. As the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, §47(b) can do coherent work as a mandatory rule of decision once rescission is properly in a case via some independent cause of action or enforcement mechanism (including SEC action or defensive invocation), and that preserves statutory coherence alongside the ICA’s selective express private remedy in §36(b). Transamerica, while relevant, doesn’t genuinely undermine that conclusion because its “void” language and pre-Sandoval approach make it an unstable foundation for implying a new ICA cause of action here.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that “may not deny rescission at the instance of any party” sounds like Congress anticipated a party coming to court affirmatively, and she worries our reading drains that phrase of operative effect. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett explain, under Sandoval and Touche Ross the key question is whether Congress clearly created a cause of action; remedial, court-directed language—even phrased in party-invoked terms—can still operate as a mandatory rule of decision once a case is properly before a court via some other claim or jurisdictional hook (including defensive rescission). Transamerica does not change that for me because it relied on materially different “void” language and predates our modern clear-statement approach, and the ICA’s structure (including the express, cabined private remedy in §36(b)) is strong textual evidence against silently adding another freestanding federal suit. So I remain with petitioner: §47(b) supplies a remedy rule, not an implied private right of action.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that “may not deny rescission at the instance of any party” sounds like Congress expected party-invoked litigation, and she warns our reading risks making that phrase inert. But under Sandoval and Touche Ross, as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, party-referential remedial language still is not rights-creating language authorizing a freestanding federal cause of action; it more naturally limits a court’s equitable discretion once rescission is otherwise properly before the court. Transamerica does not materially change that analysis because it relied on distinct “void” language and arose in a different implied-right era, and extending it here would be a substantial expansion in a statute with an SEC-centered enforcement design and selective express private remedies like §36(b). Institutionally, the narrow approach—no standalone federal cause of action in §47(b), while preserving §47(b) as a rule of decision where an independent claim/jurisdiction exists—best respects precedent and Congress’s enforcement choices.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is textual: “may not deny rescission at the instance of any party” naturally contemplates a party seeking rescission, and reading §47(b)(2) as inert risks undercutting that phrasing. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, Sandoval and Touche Ross require clear, rights-creating authorization for a freestanding federal cause of action, and §47(b)(2) reads as a court-directed remedial constraint that can operate as a rule of decision once rescission is properly before a court on some other basis (including defensive rescission, diversity, or SEC enforcement). Transamerica, as Justice Kagan notes, is materially distinguishable because it turned on “void” language and predates our modern clear-statement approach to implied causes of action; extending it would clash with the ICA’s structure, including its express, cabined private remedy in §36(b). On an originalist/textualist account, I cannot treat remedial limits on judicial discretion as silent creation of a new federal suit.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that §47(b)(2)’s “may not deny rescission at the instance of any party” sounds party-initiated, and reading it as inert absent another cause of action risks emptying that phrase of meaning. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Sandoval and Touche Ross require clearer rights-creating language than a remedial directive to courts, even one framed in terms of party invocation; the phrase can still do work as a mandatory rule of decision once rescission is properly before a court through some other claim or jurisdictional hook. Transamerica is not enough to tip me because it relied on distinct “void” language and an earlier implied-right methodology, and implying a new federal cause of action here would undercut the ICA’s selective, express private-enforcement choices (notably §36(b)). Given my focus on procedural fairness and institutional legitimacy, I remain unwilling to judicially create a freestanding enforcement pathway with significant litigation consequences absent clearer congressional authorization.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under our modern implied-right-of-action cases, the question is whether Congress clearly manifested an intent to create a private cause of action in the statute’s text and structure, not whether such a remedy would be useful. Alexander v. Sandoval and Touche Ross counsel that remedial language and judicially manageable standards are insufficient absent rights-creating terms; Section 47(b)(2)’s directive that a court “may not deny rescission at the instance of any party” can operate as a rule governing remedies for parties already properly before a court (including as a defense), without creating a new federal cause of action. The ICA’s overall structure—providing express enforcement mechanisms and limited express private remedies elsewhere—cuts against implying additional private litigation authority here. Transamerica Mortgage Advisors supports, at most, a narrow inference where statutory language unmistakably contemplates a private rescission action, but Section 47(b) is materially different and does not supply the requisite rights-creating indication of congressional intent.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 47(b) lacks the rights-creating language and clear textual indication of congressional intent that this Court requires before recognizing an implied private cause of action; at most, it addresses the legal effect or voidability of contracts and the availability of rescission as a remedy when some other properly authorized enforcement action is brought. Under Alexander v. Sandoval and Touche Ross, courts may not create private remedies from remedial language absent an affirmative statutory command, especially where the Act’s structure supplies express enforcement mechanisms and limited express private remedies elsewhere, indicating Congress knew how to authorize private suits when it wished. Section 47(b)(2)’s reference to a party “seek[ing] rescission” does not itself create a freestanding federal cause of action, and reading it to do so would expand private litigation beyond the statute’s text. Transamerica Mortgage Advisors is distinguishable because it inferred a limited remedy from different statutory text (§215 of the IAA) and does not permit implying broader private enforcement under the ICA absent similarly clear rights-conferring language.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 47(b)(2) does more than state an abstract consequence of illegality; it directs that a court "may not deny rescission at the instance of any party" absent specified equitable findings, language that most naturally presupposes a party-initiated suit for rescission in federal court. That reading is reinforced by Transamerica Mortgage Advisors, Inc. v. Lewis, which held that materially similar “void” language in IAA §215(b) "fairly implies" a limited private right to rescission and related equitable relief, while refusing to imply broader damages remedies from other provisions. Under Sandoval and Touche Ross, courts do not create new private rights absent textual indication, but here Congress’s remedy-focused text in §47(b)(2)—especially as amended to make rescission language more explicit—supplies the requisite indication of a narrow cause of action. Limiting the implied remedy to rescission (not damages) also respects the ICA’s enforcement structure and avoids expanding private litigation beyond what the text supports.
